title: Board-pattern readiness test — most-repeated question types
chapter: CBSE Class 10 Social Science (087) · Economics: Understanding Economic Development · Crash revision (2026-27)
tagline: Practice questions modelled on past CBSE papers; not predictions of this year's paper.
disclaimer: Original questions written from this video's script, its worksheet and the NCERT/CBSE material it cites, modelled on most-repeated / high-weightage question types in CBSE Sample Question Papers and past board papers. Practice for readiness only: not predictions of any exam and no promise of marks.
instructions: 35 questions. MCQ and assertion-reason: choose one option. Numeric: type a whole number (no commas needed).

S1.name: Development
S1.tip: Per capita income = total income ÷ population, but averages hide disparities. Add IMR, literacy and NAR (Kerala beats richer Haryana). HDI = health + education + income. Backward averages: total = average × number, then subtract.
S1.ncert: NCERT Understanding Economic Development (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 1 Development

S2.name: Sectors of the Indian Economy
S2.tip: GDP counts final goods only (no double counting) and = primary + secondary + tertiary. Tertiary is the largest producer; primary the largest employer → disguised unemployment. Organised vs unorganised; public vs private.
S2.ncert: NCERT Understanding Economic Development (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 2 Sectors of the Indian Economy

S3.name: Money and Credit
S3.tip: Money solves the double coincidence of wants. RBI issues notes and supervises formal lenders. Terms of credit: interest, collateral, documents, repayment. Lack of collateral pushes the poor to informal lenders; SHGs fill the gap.
S3.ncert: NCERT Understanding Economic Development (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 3 Money and Credit

S4.name: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
S4.tip: Board tests only 'what is globalisation' and 'factors that enabled it': technology (containers, air transport, ICT), liberalisation (around 1991) and international organisations (WTO). One point each + how they reinforce each other.
S4.ncert: NCERT Understanding Economic Development (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 4 Globalisation, first two sub-topics only

questions.question: The World Bank's main criterion for comparing countries is per capita income, which is:
questions.explanation: Per capita (average) income = total income ÷ population.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Total income of the country divided by its total population

questions.question: A small country of 4 people has a total income of ₹60,000. What is its per capita income in ₹?
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: The average income of 5 families is ₹8,000. Four of them earn ₹6,000, ₹9,000, ₹7,000 and ₹5,000. What does the fifth family earn, in ₹?
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: In country A, five citizens earn ₹10,000 each. In country B, four citizens earn ₹500 each and one earns ₹48,000. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: A: 50,000 ÷ 5 = 10,000. B: (2,000 + 48,000) ÷ 5 = 10,000. Same average; averages hide disparities.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: A has a higher average income than B
Both have equal distribution of income
B has a higher average income than A
Both have the same average income, but income in B is far more unequal

questions.question: The infant mortality rate (IMR) is:
questions.explanation: IMR: deaths before age 1 per 1,000 live births.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: The number of children who die before the age of five, per 100 births
The share of children aged 7+ who can read
The number of hospitals per 1,000 people
The number of children who die before the age of one year, per 1,000 live children born in that year

questions.question: Kerala has a lower per capita income than Haryana, yet a much lower infant mortality rate (6 against 28 in 2020). The main reason is:
questions.explanation: Money cannot buy every public good; public provision of health, education and PDS matters.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Kerala has adequate basic health and education facilities and a working public distribution system

questions.question: The UNDP's Human Development Report compares countries on:
questions.explanation: HDI combines health, education and income; the World Bank uses per capita income alone.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Health, education and per capita income

questions.question: A big dam would give more electricity to industries. Which group is most likely to have a conflicting developmental goal?
questions.explanation: Different people have different, sometimes conflicting, goals: one person's development can be another's loss.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Tribal people who would be displaced and may prefer small check dams
City people who want more electricity

questions.question: Which of these is a non-renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Crude oil gets exhausted after use; groundwater is renewable but can be overused.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Development; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Dairy farming belongs to which sector?
questions.explanation: Primary activities use natural resources directly: agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: A country's GDP is ₹1,200 crore. The primary sector produces ₹250 crore and the secondary sector ₹350 crore. What does the tertiary sector produce, in ₹ crore?
questions.explanation: GDP = primary + secondary + tertiary, so tertiary = 1,200 − 250 − 350 = ₹600 crore.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for ₹50, the miller sells flour to a baker for ₹80, and the baker sells biscuits to consumers for ₹150. Which value (in ₹) is counted in GDP?
questions.explanation: Only final goods count: the ₹150 biscuits already include the value of the flour and wheat. Adding 50 + 80 + 150 would be double counting.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: A family of six works on a small plot that needs only three people. If three leave, output does not fall. This is:
questions.explanation: More people are working than needed; their contribution is hidden.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which statement about India's sectors is correct?
questions.explanation: Primary employs more than half the workers yet produces only about one-sixth of GVA.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: All three sectors are equal in output and jobs
The tertiary sector is the largest producer, but the primary sector is still the largest employer
The primary sector is the largest producer and the smallest employer
The secondary sector employs more than half the workers

questions.question: Which measure would best create more work for rural people without moving them to cities?
questions.explanation: Irrigation, roads, storage, cheap credit, agro-industries and jobs in education, health and tourism.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Building rural roads and storage, and setting up agro-processing industries in semi-rural areas
Moving every farmer to a factory overnight

questions.question: Under MGNREGA 2005, how many days of work a year did the law promise to rural households?
questions.explanation: 100 days of work a year, or an unemployment allowance.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which is a feature of the organised sector?
questions.explanation: Organised: registered, follows rules and laws, regular work; unorganised: insecure, often unregistered.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: It has no rules or regulations
Enterprises are registered and give regular jobs with assured terms of employment
Jobs are low-paid and insecure with no paid leave

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true, and R is one of the four reasons for the growth of services (also basic services, support for agriculture and industry, IT).
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Sectors of the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: The tertiary sector is becoming more important in India.
questions.reason: Rising incomes create demand for services such as eating out, tourism and private schools.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: In a barter system, the main problem is the need for:
questions.explanation: Both sides must want exactly what the other has; money removes this by acting as a medium of exchange.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Who issues currency notes in India on behalf of the central government?
questions.explanation: The RBI issues notes; no one in India can legally refuse the rupee.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: A bank keeps about 5% of its deposits as cash. If people deposit ₹2,00,000, how much (in ₹) does it keep as cash?
questions.explanation: 5% of 2,00,000 = ₹10,000; the rest is lent out.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Collateral is:
questions.explanation: Land, a building, vehicle, livestock or deposits; the lender can sell it if the loan is not repaid.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: The interest charged on a loan
An asset the borrower owns and pledges to the lender until the loan is repaid

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the terms of credit?
questions.explanation: Terms of credit: interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: The number of bank branches in the city

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true; lack of collateral (R) is a key reason they turn to moneylenders (A).
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: Poor households depend largely on informal sources of credit.
questions.reason: They often lack the collateral and documents that banks require.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Ravi borrows from a moneylender at a high interest rate to grow a crop. The crop fails, and he has to sell part of his land to repay. This situation is called:
questions.explanation: Credit that cannot be repaid pushes the borrower into a worse situation: a debt trap.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: A self-help group (SHG) usually has:
questions.explanation: After a year or two of saving, the group can borrow from a bank; group pressure ensures repayment.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: 15 to 20 members, mostly women, who save regularly

questions.question: Why does the RBI supervise formal lenders?
questions.explanation: RBI monitors cash balances and lending, so credit reaches small borrowers too; nobody supervises informal lenders.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Money and Credit; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: To check that banks keep enough cash balance and also lend to small cultivators and small industries
To set the price of vegetables

questions.question: A multinational corporation (MNC) is a company that:
questions.explanation: MNCs spread production across countries.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Sells only in its own city
Owns or controls production in more than one nation

questions.question: Globalisation is best described as:
questions.explanation: Goods, services, investment and technology move across borders; people move less because of restrictions.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Moving all people to one country
Rapid integration or interconnection between countries through trade and investment

questions.question: In globalisation, which moves LEAST freely between countries?
questions.explanation: People move less because of various restrictions.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a trade barrier?
questions.explanation: A tax on imports restricts trade; the others are technology factors that help trade.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Around which year did India remove barriers on foreign trade and investment to a large extent?
questions.explanation: Around 1991, so Indian producers would compete globally and improve quality.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true, and R explains A; developed countries also protected their producers in their early stages.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: After independence, the Indian government restricted foreign trade and investment.
questions.reason: It wanted to protect young domestic producers from foreign competition.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Which is a LIBERALISATION factor in globalisation, rather than a technology factor?
questions.explanation: Liberalisation = removing government barriers; the others are improvements in technology.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Removing government barriers on imports and investment

questions.question: How has information and communication technology helped globalisation?
questions.explanation: Telecom, computers, the internet and satellites let services be produced and paid for across borders.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Globalisation and the Indian Economy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: It has made transport costs higher
It has stopped trade between countries
A magazine for London can be designed in Delhi and paid for instantly by e-banking
